steps.label: Set up sin2θ = cos3θ
steps.margin_note: First mark. 18° is one fifth of 90°, so 2θ and 3θ are complementary and sin2θ = cos3θ. Expand both sides.
steps.memory_tip: 18° is one fifth of 90°, so 2θ = 90° − 3θ and sin2θ = cos3θ.
lines: Use the double- and triple-angle formulas:

recall.must_convey: That 5θ = 90° gives 2θ = 90° − 3θ, so sin2θ = cos3θ, and both sides are expanded.
accept: five theta is ninety so two theta and three theta are complementary
sin two theta equals cos three theta
expand as two sin theta cos theta equals four cos cubed minus three cos
five theta ninety kabatti sin two theta equals cos three theta
eighteen is one fifth of ninety

steps.why: 18° is one fifth of 90°. That is the only special fact about it, and it is what turns the question into an equation that can be solved.
common_mistakes: Using cos2θ = sin3θ, which is also true but gives a cubic in sinθ with an extra root sinθ = 1 to discard.

steps.label: Solve the quadratic in sinθ
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Divide by cosθ (which is not zero at 18°), replace cos²θ by 1 − sin²θ, and take the positive root because 18° is acute.
steps.memory_tip: 4sin²θ + 2 sinθ − 1 = 0. Take the positive root, because 18° is acute.

recall.must_convey: That dividing by cosθ and replacing cos²θ gives 4sin²θ + 2 sinθ − 1 = 0, whose positive root is (√5 − 1)/4.
accept: divide by cos theta and replace cos squared by one minus sin squared
the quadratic is four sin squared plus two sin theta minus one equals zero
the roots are minus one plus or minus root five over four
eighteen acute kabatti positive root theeskovali
so sin eighteen is root five minus one by four

steps.why: Replacing cos²θ by 1 − sin²θ leaves one unknown, so the equation becomes an ordinary quadratic. The quadrant then decides which of its two roots is wanted.
common_mistakes: Dividing by cosθ without saying it is not zero.
